title: Doubled consonants
summary: Five tense doubles: no puff of air, a tight start.

sections.p: Doubled ㄲ ㄸ ㅃ ㅆ ㅉ sit in the same mouth positions as ㄱ ㄷ ㅂ ㅅ ㅈ but the start is tight, with almost no air. English has nothing quite like them; keep the mouth small and the start short.
examples: house — compare ㅂ in 받침 later

sections.p: Do not confuse ㅋ with ㄲ: ㅋ is a puff, ㄲ is tense. In these lessons romanization uses doubled letters: tt, ss, pp, jj, kk.

drills.why: ㄸ is doubled ㄷ, not aspirated ㅌ.
ㄲ is tense; ㅋ is aspirated.

drills.q: Which pair is plain versus tense?
drills.why: ㅃ is the tense partner of ㅂ.
집 is jip, one ㅈ not doubled.

title: Combined vowels
particle: ㅘ ㅙ ㅚ ㅝ ㅞ ㅟ ㅢ
summary: Vowels built from two parts; yot marks ㅑ ㅕ ㅛ ㅠ inside a bigger vowel.

sections.p: After a consonant, ㅘ wa, ㅙ wae, ㅚ oe, ㅝ wo, ㅞ we, ㅟ wi, ㅢ ui are one vowel sound in one block. ㅚ and ㅟ are often pronounced like we and wi in modern Seoul speech.
Like simple vowels, combined vowels are tall and stand to the right: 과 is ㄱ + ㅘ.

drills.why: 과 stacks ㄱ with the combined vowel ㅘ.
ㅝ is wo, as in the question word (rare alone).

drills.q: Combined vowels in a block sit…
options: to the right of the first consonant
drills.answer: to the right of the first consonant

title: Numbers 1–10
summary: Native Korean numbers for counting small things and telling age in speech.

sections.p: 하나, 둘, 셋, 넷, 다섯, 여섯, 일곱, 여덟, 아홉, 열 are the native numbers one to ten. Before a counter they shorten: 한, 두, 세, 네 (하나→한, 둘→두…).

drills.why: 셋 becomes 세 before a counter.

drills.q: Which is the native word for four?

title: Sino-Korean numbers
summary: Chinese-origin numbers for dates, money, floors and phone digits.

sections.p: 일, 이, 삼, 사, 오, 육, 칠, 팔, 구, 십 are the Sino-Korean digits. They combine for larger numbers: 십일 eleven, 이십 twenty, 삼십오 thirty-five.

drills.why: 층 is floor; 이층 second floor.

title: Greetings
summary: Hello, goodbye and thank you in polite speech.

sections.p: 안녕하세요 is hello. 안녕히 가세요 says goodbye to someone leaving; 안녕히 계세요 to someone staying. 감사합니다 is thank you; 천만에요 answers it.

drills.why: 안녕하세요 is the everyday polite hello.

drills.q: Someone leaves your shop. You say…
You stay; the guest leaves. They say to you…

sections.p: 네 (often pronounced ne or e) means yes. 아니요 means no. 아니에요 softens “that's not so” or “I'm not”.

drills.why: 네 is yes in everyday polite speech.

title: Reading: body and health
summary: Common body words in Hangul blocks.

sections.p: Read each block left to right, top to bottom: 머리 meori head, 손 son hand, 발 bal foot, 눈 nun eye, 귀 gwi ear.

drills.why: 눈 nun is eye (context also snow).

title: Reading: food words
summary: Everyday food vocabulary in syllable blocks.

sections.p: 밥 bap cooked rice/meal, 물 mul water, 김치 gimchi kimchi, 불고기 bulgogi, 빵 ppang bread.

drills.why: 밥 bap is cooked rice or a meal.

sections.p: 집 jip home, 학교 hakgyo school, 병원 byeongwon hospital, 공원 gongwon park, 회사 hoesa company.
도 after a noun means also, too, or even. It replaces 은/는 or 을/를 when those roles apply: 저도 “me too”, 커피도 “coffee too”.

drills.q: 도 replaces which pair when marking also on a topic?
drills.why: Topic also: noun + 도 instead of 는.

sections.p: 만 means only or just: 커피만 “only coffee”, 오늘만 “only today”.

drills.q: 만 versus 도: which excludes others?
drills.why: 만 is only; 도 is also.

sections.p: 에게 (written) and 한테 (spoken) mark the person who receives an action: 친구에게 전화해요 “I call a friend”. Animals and very polite speech use different words; start with people.
examples: I gave a gift to a friend.

drills.why: 한테 is spoken to a person.
한테 is colloquial; 에게 is neutral/written.

drills.q: I gave Mom a gift: 엄마＿ 선물.

title: 에 — time and schedule
summary: Clock time and fixed appointments take 에.

sections.p: Hours and days take 에: 세 시에 at three, 월요일에 on Monday, 내일에 tomorrow (often 내일 alone).

drills.why: 내일 can stand without 에 in speech.

title: Question words
summary: What, where, who, when in basic questions.

sections.p: 뭐 (무엇) what, 어디 where, 누구 who, 언제 when. They stay in the sentence; the verb still ends the clause.

title: 주세요 and 죄송합니다
summary: Please give me… and a basic apology.

sections.p: 주세요 is please give (me): 커피 주세요 “Coffee, please.” 죄송합니다 is I'm sorry (polite). 미안합니다 is also sorry, slightly less formal in some settings.

title: -아/어 주세요 — please do for me
summary: Ask someone to do something for you politely.

sections.p: Stem + -아/어 주세요 asks a favor: 앉아 주세요 means please sit. The same vowel rule as -아요/-어요.

title: -아/어서 — and so / because (spoken)
summary: Spoken reason and sequence; same vowel rule as -아요.

sections.p: -아서 / -어서 links clauses in speech. Tense goes on the final verb only.
examples: I was hungry, so I ate.
I was tired, so I slept early.

title: 더 — more
summary: Put 더 before an adjective for comparison.

sections.p: 더 before an adjective means more. A보다 marks the standard in comparisons.
-아/어도 돼요? asks permission. 안 돼요 is not allowed.

title: 그런데 / 그리고 — by the way, and

sections.p: 그리고 adds another fact. 그런데 changes topic or adds contrast.

title: -아/어 보다 — try doing
summary: Try an action to see what it is like.

sections.p: Stem + -아/어 보다 tries something. Past: 먹어 봤어요 I tried eating.

drills.q: Try eating once: 한번 먹＿ 보세요.

sections.p: Pattern in context: -다고. Example: 민수가 온{다고} 했어요..
Pattern in context: -기 전에. Example: 먹{기 전에}.
Pattern in context: -고 나서. Example: 먹{고 나서}.
Pattern in context: -는데. Example: 비가 오{는데}.
Pattern in context: -니까. Example: 바쁘{니까}.
Pattern in context: -면. Example: 시간이 있{으면}.
Pattern in context: -기. Example: {먹기}.
Pattern in context: -이/히. Example: 문이 {열렸어요}.
Use -(으)시- for elder/subject honorific: 오{세요}.
주시다 honorific of 주다.
드시다 replaces 먹다 for elders.
드리다 humble give; 여쭙다 humble ask.
-님 after roles: 선생님, 사장님.
께 to person; 께서 subject honorific.
말씀 for respected speech.
Ask age with 연세, name with 성함.
처음 뵙겠습니다; 잘 부탁드립니다.
Plain present -ㄴ다/-는다.
Formal -ㅂ니다/-습니다.
News uses -되다 passives.
Headlines drop particles.
바로 precisely; 즉 that is.
…것으로 보인다; …알려졌다.
Modifiers before nouns: 읽는 책.
Notices use -(으)므로.
Plain reports use -다고 with plain matrix.
